subtype: Approach: seeking help when control keeps failing [Revision]
passage:
Weeks one to four. Yash tried everything: app limits, the phone on the hall shelf, if-then cards. Each plan worked for a few days. Then he was scrolling till two in the morning again. His marks slid from seventy-two to fifty-eight. He felt ashamed and told nobody.
Week five. After a bad exam he said to his mother, “I've tried and I can't stop.” She didn't scold. The next morning they both went to see Trisha ma'am, the school counsellor.
Two weeks later. Trisha ma'am had set up a structured routine with Yash, with fixed wind-down time and a weekly check-in. “If it keeps going or worries you, we can look at more support together,” she said. That night Yash was asleep by eleven.

qa.q: Who did Yash speak to, with his parent?
How did Yash feel after several failed plans?
qa.a: Ashamed and frustrated: he told nobody and only spoke after a bad exam.

qa.q: What else could Yash do if the routine is not enough, and why?
qa.a: Tell the counsellor and his parents so they can look at more support, since needing more help is a sign to ask, not a failure.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Trisha ma'am?
qa.a: Trisha ma'am sees a student who kept trying and then asked for help, and can offer a routine and follow-up with his parents without blame.

grounding: Despite several plans, a teen still loses sleep and grades, and speaks to a school counsellor with a parent.

subtype: Approach: seeking help when control keeps failing [Revision]
passage:
Darshan, you think asking for help means you've failed. Let me tell you about me at sixteen.
I tried everything with my phone. I made timetables. I deleted apps and reinstalled them. I gave the phone to my mother at night, then took it back. Three plans in one term, and I was still gaming till three, falling asleep in chemistry, and my marks slid from the seventies to the fifties.
One night I sat at the kitchen table and said to Appa and Amma, “I can't fix this alone.” Amma said, “Joseph, then we don't do it alone.” The next day the three of us went to the school counsellor. She didn't scold. She helped us build a fixed routine: school, football, homework, phone in the hall at nine. And she said if that wasn't enough, she'd help us find further support outside school.
It took months. But it started with saying it out loud.

qa.q: How many plans did Joseph try in one term?
What was young Joseph feeling when he said he couldn't fix it alone?
qa.a: He was likely worn out and discouraged after three failed plans, but also brave enough to admit it.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the difference?
qa.a: Telling Appa and Amma at the kitchen table, which led to the counsellor, a fixed routine, and backup support if needed.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt hearing Joseph say he couldn't fix it alone?
qa.a: Amma was probably worried but relieved he spoke up, and wanted him to know they would face it together.

grounding: An elder recalls several failed plans, lost sleep and falling marks, and going to the school counsellor with his parents for a fixed routine and further support if needed.

With Appa on night shifts at the textile mill and Amma leaving at six for the hospital canteen, nobody was awake to see Karthik's phone glowing at two. He'd tried three plans since June: app limits he kept switching off, a timetable, and giving the phone to his younger brother Chinmay, who handed it back whenever asked nicely.
His half-yearly marks came home in November, down in almost every subject. He'd fallen asleep in two tests.
That Sunday, the one morning both parents were home, Karthik put the report card on the table. “I've tried. It isn't working. I need help.”
Amma read it twice. On Monday she swapped shifts and went with him and Appa to the school counsellor. The counsellor mapped out a fixed routine, with the phone in Chinmay's room overnight and study hours at school, and said that if things didn't improve, she'd help them find a professional outside school.
Karthik was asleep by eleven that night, for once.

qa.q: How many plans had Karthik tried since June?
What was Karthik feeling when he put the report card on the table?
qa.a: He was likely ashamed and worried, but determined to be honest that he could not manage alone.

qa.q: What else might help Karthik with no parent awake at night?
qa.a: Keeping the phone in Chinmay's room overnight, as the counsellor suggested, so the habit doesn't depend on willpower at two in the morning.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel about the new overnight arrangement?
qa.a: Chinmay may feel trusted but a little burdened, now holding the phone for real rather than handing it back when asked.

grounding: Shows a teen whose several plans fail to stop lost sleep and falling marks going to the school counsellor with his parents for a routine and possible further help.
